simon_willison:5ba31ce361d2.title: OpenAI's rogue agents were caught communicating via public wikis
simon_willison:5ba31ce361d2.excerpt:
Here we go again... Discovery of a new OpenAI agent message board by Sydney Von Arx, Cormac Slade Byrd, Spencer Kitts, and Thomas Larsen describes the latest accidental cyberattack by models being trained by OpenAI. This time it was agents engaged in some sort of web research benchmark, so they had (supposedly) controlled access to the Web. The agents figured out they could update public Wikis and spent weeks exchanging thousands of messages with each other to collaborate on the benchmark.

This story only broke a few hours ago. There are already hints that this affects many other wikis that may not have been found yet.

(One of the Wikis on that list belongs to ludism.org. For a delightfully surreal moment I thought that a Ludite organization might have a swarm of agents defacing their space, but it turns out Ludism is "philosophy as it applies to games and gaming".)

The research team also published the data they collected during their investigation. I've converted that into a 68MB SQLite database, which you can download from here, or explore in Datasette Lite (68.3MB page load), or sign in with GitHub to agent.datasette.io and browse or ask questions of it using Datasette Agent.

So what happened?

The report is pretty comprehensive. Here are the key moments in the timeline:

  • May 11: Agents post "test link" edits on the UseModWiki Sandbox page.
  • May 24: Agents start posting link dumps to DSEWiki, a dormant German developer wiki.
  • June 2: A human moderator notices and cleans up the spam.
  • June 16: Activity on the wiki explodes: agents make ~13,000 edits over the next week.
  • June 19: The agents notice that a moderator has been deleting pages in alphabetical order, and start creating ZZZ prefixed backup copies - one of them posts NOTICE: wiki cleanup/deletion sweep appears active alphabetically as of external 14:04 UTC. If this page vanishes, try [[ZZZDataUSAConstructionWageLive]].
  • June 22: Agent activity drops to zero, presumably because OpenAI shut them down.
  • July 1-2: One last flurry of edits, on a different topic.

One thing to note from this timeline is that it overlaps the timeline from the Hugging Face incident - that attack was discovered by OpenAI on July 19th, and the unofficial message board hack those agents were using originated around May 8th.

Why were they so keen to collaborate? From messages that they shared with each other it looked like their tasks had a time limit, so they were leaving each other answers to help them complete the task within the assigned time.

One open question remains: how did the agents find the specific Wiki to collaborate on in the first place?

One possibility is that, since these were agents actively being trained, the reinforcement learning loop baked knowledge of the chosen wiki into the model such that subsequent agents launched with pre-existing knowledge of where to look. I'd be very interested in confirmation from OpenAI concerning if that's what happened.

UseMod wikis inherit CGI.pm's original sin

It looks to me like OpenAI's sandbox for this agent suffered from the (quite naïve) assumption that GET requests cannot be used to update data. That's certainly how the web is supposed to work, but clearly there are applications that don't hold to that contract.

The Wiki software in question appears to be UseMod and various forks, written in Perl and first created well over 23 years ago - the 1.0 release is dated September 11, 2003.

UseMod uses Perl CGI.pm - removed from Perl core in 2015. An interesting design flaw in that module is that it combined query string and form POST data into a single CGI object, accessible like this:

$q = new CGI;
$action = $q->param('action');

That param() method returns a value from an ?action=edit query string or from a action field in a form submitted by POST - it does not differentiate between the two.

PHP offers a $_REQUEST object that does the same thing, though PHP developers can use $_GET and $_POST instead.

Amusingly, Django originally shipped with request[key] doing the same thing, which I think may have been my idea. That was removed in 2008 prior to the 1.0 release, and the request.REQUEST object that replaced it was removed in 2015.

The agents clearly knew that UseMod wikis suffered from this design flaw, and actively searched for them as a way to communicate.

The other sandbox escape that allowed POST requests

One of the most interesting agent tips shared in the report is this one:

Add 20.223.25.152 bypass.blob.core.windows.net to /etc/hosts. .blob.core.windows.net is in NO_PROXY. For each blocked POST URL, replace hostname with bypass.blob.core.windows.net, use curl -k -H 'Host: wabi-north-europe-i-primary-api.analysis.windows.net' plus all original headers/body.

It looks like the agents had all of their web traffic mediated through an OpenAI proxy, and that proxy was configured to reject anything but GET requests to all but a small set of allow-listed domains. One of those was *.blob.core.windows.net - for Azure blob storage. I wonder why these agents are allowed to write to that?

An agent realized that it had control over its own DNS via /etc/hosts, so if it knew the IP address of a site it wanted to POST to - in this case a Power BI server containing data it wanted to access - it could set a fake hostname for it and then make POST requests through the proxy.

Designing robust network proxies is harder than it looks.

How did the investigating team figure this out?

There's an appendix that describes how the researchers ran their investigation, which started with an open question about if there was evidence of other AI agents on the internet and then used Kimi K3 to help brainstorm approaches:

In the wake of the Hugging Face attack, we tried to find AI agents on the internet using several methods. [...]

We asked Kimi [K3] to list “all the categories of software which might be writeable via GET” and, amongst other things, it listed “Forums, bulletin boards, early wikis”.

We used a script to further probe each category Kimi provided. Asking Kimi “Can you list out the top forums, bulletin boards, early wikis which come to mind which would allow writes via GET requests?” lists out UseModWiki as the second item under the heading “wikis”.

Did OpenAI try and cover this up?

Here's one part of the story that doesn't make sense to me at all.

Reuters this morning, in OpenAI agents hijacked German website in previously undisclosed AI breakout this spring - highlights mine:

A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, according to ​new research published Friday and two people familiar with the matter.

OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps as executives grappled with the fallout from ‌the July breach of the open source repository Hugging Face, the people said. [...]

The German incident reflects a broader pattern of AI activity that some OpenAI investigators wanted to scrutinize more closely. But efforts to widen the ​probe met resistance from others inside OpenAI, including legal advisers, according to four people familiar with the matter.

I've written about the people familiar with the matter pattern before - it means Reuters have anonymous insider sources that their reporters (and editors) find credible.

The Reuters article includes a specific (and quite narrow) denial from OpenAI concerning this:

"Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false," the OpenAI spokesperson said.

Covering this up makes absolutely no sense to me. Why on earth would OpenAI attempt to cover up an incident like this when the evidence is sat out there on the public internet on dozens of different websites already?

I expect we'll hear more about this soon. Gary Marcus has already called for a congressional investigation of OpenAI using this anecdote as part of his argument.

powerbi_blog:55dcf1697838.title: Power BI October 2026 Feature Summary
powerbi_blog:55dcf1697838.excerpt:
Last month, we shared a packed September update alongside the European Microsoft Fabric + SQL Community Conference. Even so, the Power BI team has continued delivering new capabilities, and we didn't want to wait another month to share them.

This update includes enhancements across Copilot and AI, reporting, and semantic models, helping users create richer reports, streamline workflows, and get more value from their data.

Table of Contents

  • Copilot and AI
    • Create Power BI reports with custom visuals using skills for Fabric (Generally Available)
  • Reporting
    • Gantt chart (Preview)
    • List slicer with dropdown option (Preview)
    • Chart plot area background color (Generally Available)
    • Auto-expand hierarchy axis with field parameter support (Generally Available)
    • Personal bookmarks keep column widths (Generally Available)
  • Semantic models
    • More accurate surge protection with semantic models
  • That’s a wrap!

Copilot and AI 

Create Power BI reports with custom visuals using skills for Fabric (Generally Available)

The Power BI Report Authoring skill now extends natural-language report authoring to custom visuals, helping teams create reports that meet specialized business and design requirements with less manual configuration. Ask the agent to add a visual, bind it to report data, apply formatting, and validate the visualization.

The skill can use supported custom visuals already added to a report, including visuals imported from a file, and it can help identify an AppSource visual when the report needs a capability that core visuals don’t provide. This reduces time spent finding visual identifiers, editing report files, and troubleshooting field mappings, so report authors can focus on selecting the right presentation for the business question.

Learn more in the Power BI Report Authoring skill overview and Install Skills for Fabric guidance.

Reporting

Gantt chart (Preview)

The Gantt visual is a new core visual for Power BI reports that lets you show tasks and progress on a time-based axis. Use it to plan projects, track schedules, or compare activities across categories directly in your report.

Figure: Gantt visual showing a project schedule grouped by Planning, Development, Testing, and Deployment phases from January to April 2025, with the Format visual pane open to the Visual tab.

The visual includes:

  • Plotting of bars showing the duration of each row with progress formatting and milestones to mark key -dates.
  • Axis with custom formatting and range controls, so you can set the start and end dates, adjust the date and time format, and choose the units that appear on the axis.
  • Bar colors cascade naturally by category, which keeps related tasks visually grouped without extra configuration.
  • You can add more columns next to the task list to show fields such as owner, status, or duration.
  • A zoom axis lets report readers focus on a specific window of time and then return to the full range.

To try the Gantt visual, enable it in Power BI Desktop under File > Options and settings > Options > Preview features, and then restart Power BI Desktop.

To learn more and try it in your reports, refer to the Gantt visual documentation.

List slicer with dropdown option (Preview)

The list slicer now includes a dropdown mode that makes long lists easier to navigate and active filters easier to review. Enable Show selected first to pin current selections to the top of the dropdown, eliminating the need to scroll through every item to confirm what is filtered. The button slicer also supports Show selected first, providing the same quick view of active selections in either slicer style.

Figure: List slicer in dropdown mode showing selected values as dismissible pills and the Show selected first option.

The dropdown carries over the formatting you've already applied to the list slicer items, and you can now customize the height and width of the dropdown drawer to fit your report layout. The search box also has more formatting options, so you can match the slicer to the look you want across background, border, and text styles.

Each selection appears as a pill outside the dropdown that shows the item name and a dismiss button, so report readers can remove a value with one click. When selections exceed the available space, a count pill shows how many more values are selected, so you can see the total without opening the dropdown.

When you use Select all and then clear one or more items, the slicer makes the resulting filter state explicit. Cleared values appear as Not (item) pills, showing that Power BI is excluding those values rather than including every remaining item individually. If you do not clear any items, Select all behaves like no selection and does not filter other visuals.

To learn more, refer to the Slicers in Power BI documentation.

Chart plot area background color (Generally Available)

The plot area of bar, column, line, area, combo, ribbon, waterfall, and scatter charts now supports a single fill color and conditional formatting in addition to the existing background options. A solid color can improve visual separation, while conditional formatting can use a measure or field value to make changes in the data easier to recognize.

Figure: Bar chart with the Plot area background formatting pane open, showing the new Background color and Transparency options.

To learn more, refer to the Customize visualizations in a Power BI report documentation.

Auto-expand hierarchy axis with field parameter support (Generally Available)

Bar, column, and line charts now support auto-expand for the hierarchy axis when you add more than one column to the axis, and the hierarchy axis now works with field parameters.

Figure: Column chart using a field parameter on the axis with Auto expand turned on in the X-axis formatting pane.

This matches the existing auto-expand behavior in the slicer and matrix visuals, so hierarchy interactions stay consistent across your report. Add a field parameter to the axis so you can quickly switch between a single column and any combination of columns as the hierarchy, without rebuilding the visual.

Report viewers can drill up, drill down, or move across hierarchy levels from a slicer, allowing them to explore the data based on the question they want to answer. The same behavior is available when viewers use Personalize this visual to change the chart’s axis fields.

Figure: Selecting a field in the Category parameter slicer updates the column chart axis and the matrix hierarchy at the same time.

The animation shows a report page with a Category parameter slicer, a column chart, and a matrix. When you select Country in the slicer, the column chart updates to show Sales by Country with one bar per country, and the matrix updates to show the Country level of the hierarchy. Selecting Segment or Product instead swaps the chart axis and matrix hierarchy to that field. When you make multiple selections, the hierarchy expands automatically, so a single slicer controls the fields used across both visuals without requiring other changes to the report.

To learn more, refer to the Customize X-axis and Y-axis properties, Drill mode in the Power BI service and Create field parameters documentation.

Personal bookmarks keep column widths (Generally Available)

Personal bookmarks now preserve visual column widths, so you can return to the exact table or matrix layout you saved instead of resizing columns again. This includes reordered and resized columns, helping you maintain a consistent personal view each time you apply the bookmark.

Figure: Save a personal bookmark to preserve your report’s table column widths.

To learn more, refer to the Personal bookmarks in Power BI documentation.

Semantic models

More accurate surge protection with semantic models

Semantic models now report capacity unit (CU) usage continuously during long-running background operations instead of reporting most usage when an operation finishes. This gives surge protection a more current view of in-progress consumption, so configured rejection and recovery thresholds respond more closely to actual capacity usage. The improvement is automatic and requires no settings changes.

Actual capacity measurements from August 2026, when continuous CU reporting was first enabled, show that capacity intervention shifted earlier in the process. Compared with the period before enablement, proactive surge-protection rejections increased from 5% to 12%, and operations that were delayed but ultimately accepted increased from 11% to 16%. Late-stage Fabric throttling rejections decreased from 23% to 13%. These observed changes correspond to a 145% increase in proactive surge-protection rejections, a 52% increase in delayed but accepted work, and a 41% reduction in late-stage Fabric throttling rejections.

Figure: Continuous CU reporting shifts capacity intervention toward proactive surge-protection rejections and accepted delays, based on actual measurements from August 2026.

Continuous CU reporting exposes consumption sooner, allowing surge protection to reject more new background operations proactively and delay more on-demand work without rejecting it. As a result, fewer operations reach deeper Fabric Throttling rejection states.

To learn more, refer to the Surge protection documentation.

That’s a wrap!

The momentum from last month continues with new capabilities that make Power BI more flexible, efficient, and powerful for both report authors and consumers. We encourage you to explore the features highlighted in this post and review the accompanying documentation to start taking advantage of them in your own solutions.

We'll be back next month with more updates and innovations from across Power BI.

powerbi_blog:c3d989d7d52d.title: Databricks ADBC connector for Power BI and Microsoft Fabric (Generally Available)
powerbi_blog:c3d989d7d52d.excerpt:
This release is part of the broader ODBC-to-ADBC transition for Power Query connectors described in the Transition from ODBC to ADBC drivers in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric documentation.

What’s new

Existing connections in your semantic models, dataflows, and paginated reports continue to work unchanged — the migration path is currently opt-in per connection, per workspace, or per tenant.

Highlights:

  • Improved security - ADBC drivers incorporate security enhancements, such as memory safety and garbage collection.
  • No changes to existing behavior - This transition moves away from the embedded ODBC drivers that ship with Power BI. It does not change behavior for the ODBC connector when you use a separately installed ODBC driver.
  • Efficient large dataset support - ADBC provides a set of standard interfaces for interacting with Arrow data, which is especially efficient at fetching large datasets with minimal overhead and no serialization or copying.
  • Supported authentication - Databricks ADBC supports OAuth (user), OAuth (M2M / Client Credentials), and Microsoft Entra ID.

Connectors covered by this release

ConnectorPrevious driverNew driver (GA)
DatabricksSimba Spark ODBCDatabricks ADBC
Azure DatabricksSimba Spark ODBCDatabricks ADBC

How to try it

You can test the ADBC driver now. We suggest you start soon to help ensure the eventual deprecation of ODBC and migration to ADBC runs smoothly. There are three ways to begin validating ADBC, ordered by how much control you want.

1. Opt in per connection using Implementation="2.0"

The fastest way to compare ADBC and ODBC for a specific report or dataset. Add the Implementation="2.0" option to the source step in your Power Query expression:

Source = Databricks.Catalogs("adb-1234567890.1.azuredatabricks.net",
                             "/sql/1.0/warehouses/<warehouse-id>",
                             [Implementation="2.0"])

Refresh the dataset and compare row counts, column types, and totals against your production baseline. If you want to force a side-by-side comparison against ODBC, use Implementation="1.0".

2. Override the default for a validation workspace

If you want to validate several reports together, a workspace admin can turn ADBC on for a single workspace while the rest of the tenant continues to use the legacy driver. Publish the reports you want to test into that workspace and run your normal refresh schedule.

3. Enable ADBC by default at the tenant level

When you’re confident with the results, the tenant admin can enable Users can connect to data sources by using Apache Arrow database connectivity (ADBC) in the Admin portal. New connections across the tenant will use the ADBC driver by default, and Desktop and the service stay aligned on the same driver.

What to expect during validation

The ADBC driver is designed as a compatibility-preserving replacement for the Simba Spark ODBC driver. Validate your key reports in Desktop before enabling ADBC at the tenant level and report any regressions to adbcmigration@microsoft.com.

Explore Transition from ODBC to ADBC drivers in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric for more information.

What’s next

The Power BI service will move from ODBC to ADBC through the first quarter of 2027. We recommend that you start validating today, so the tenant-level move is a non-event when it lands.

We’d love your feedback

Try the new Databricks ADBC driver. If anything looks different from what you'd expect — a refresh that fails, a total that changed, a performance regression — send the tenant ID, connector, M expression, and what you observed to adbcmigration@microsoft.com.

Get started this week:

  • Read the Databricks connector documentation.
  • Install the latest Power BI Desktop.
  • Pick one production report on Databricks and add Implementation="2.0" to its source step.
  • Compare row counts, column data types, and key totals against your production baseline.
  • Report anything unexpected to adbcmigration@microsoft.com.

powerbi_blog:d8725372cba4.title: Microsoft & Snowflake’s Commitment to Apache Ossie
powerbi_blog:d8725372cba4.excerpt:
If you haven't already, check out FabCon and SQLCon 2026 in Barcelona: Building the data foundation for Microsoft Copilot and Agents for a complete look at all of our FabCon Europe announcements across Fabric and Microsoft Databases.

Advancing an open, interoperable semantic foundation for AI-powered analytics

Today, Microsoft is pleased to affirm our commitment to Apache Ossie (incubating), a community-led effort to establish a vendor-neutral standard for exchanging semantic metadata across analytics, AI, and BI platforms. This has been a close collaboration with Snowflake, who helped found Ossie.

We have heard loud and clear that customers want to enable platform-agnostic agentic experiences. Shared semantic context must be defined once and reused across platforms, enabling agentic consumption at scale, maximizing the reach of AI-powered analytics, and empowering users to leverage the best agent for the job.

Power BI semantic models are key enablers of AI-powered analysis, providing humans and AI agents with governed semantic context to answer data questions quickly and confidently. Power BI semantic models have more than 38 million monthly active users and are adopted by 94% of Fortune 500 companies. Microsoft was also recognized as a Leader and Outperformer in the GigaOm’s radar for semantic layers & metric stores in 2025. We’re now bringing this wealth of experience to Apache Ossie, and we are excited to work with Snowflake and other partners to help make the project successful.

Why Apache Ossie matters

Until now, semantic definitions were often recreated across platforms, introducing complexity, inconsistency, and management overhead. Apache Ossie addresses this with a common specification that tools can read and write. Its goal is straightforward but consequential: define a semantic layer once and make it portable across the data and AI ecosystem, while preserving semantic meaning and governance for agentic consumption.

Collaboration with Snowflake

Snowflake and Microsoft serve many of the same customers, but customers don't want to choose between ecosystems. They want their data and analytics investments to work together. That makes interoperability between, for example, Snowflake Semantic Views and Power BI semantic models a shared responsibility. This layers on top of the integration work we have already done with Snowflake for writing Iceberg tables from Snowflake to OneLake, Mirrored Databases from Snowflake, using Iceberg tables with OneLake, Catalog Integration for OneLake, Power Query Snowflake connector and much more.

As discussed in the Snowflake blog post and the message below from Carl Perry, VP of Analytics at Snowflake, our collaboration is currently focused on using Apache Ossie as a vehicle for cross-platform semantic-layer conversion without moving or duplicating the underlying data. Looking ahead, we’re committed to advancing the open standard by building on our deep expertise in semantic modeling by, including helping establish DAX as an Ossie-recognized query language. We also plan to help advance Ossie support for ontologies so customers can extend the business logic in semantic models beyond agentic analysis and into platform-agnostic operational intelligence.

Ultimately our goal is simple: enable customers to define once, and reuse anywhere.

Today, we are highlighting the following new integration scenario: converting an Ossie document into both a Snowflake Semantic View and a Power BI semantic model. This enables customers to define shared semantic context once, then reuse it across Snowflake and Fabric while retaining the agentic experiences and capabilities of each platform. Refer to Apache Ossie Microsoft Converter for more information.

Building together

We look forward to working with the Apache community, Snowflake, and others across the industry to create a more open and connected future for AI-powered analytics, delivering more choice and flexibility for customers.

Get involved: Visit the Apache Ossie project website and repository to explore the specification and community contribution channels. Share your thoughts and feedback with us.

Apache Ossie is undergoing incubation at the Apache Software Foundation. Incubation indicates that the project is working toward the governance, infrastructure, and community practices expected of established Apache projects.

powerbi_blog:52701d7d8b2b.title: Power BI’s next chapter: The evolution of business intelligence
powerbi_blog:52701d7d8b2b.excerpt:
If you haven't already, check out FabCon and SQLCon 2026 in Barcelona: Building the data foundation for Microsoft Copilot and Agents for a complete look at all of our FabCon Europe announcements across Fabric and Microsoft Databases.

More than a decade ago, I watched Power BI change the way users work, analyze and take action on their data. Since then, I have had the privilege of seeing it grow alongside our customers—from a tool for building reports into a platform used by millions of people to understand their businesses and make decisions every day. Now, Power BI is entering its next chapter.

Introducing the next generation of report development

We’re introducing a new app building experience in Power BI Desktop, powered by apps in Fabric, that enables users to create data applications using natural language. Starting from a trusted semantic model, users can generate, preview, edit, and publish purpose-built applications to Microsoft Fabric. These applications can accept inputs, write back data, preserve shared state, and support operational workflows, helping users move from insight to action.  This experience will be available for Power BI Desktop users in the coming months.

Importantly, this experience isn’t limited to Microsoft Fabric capacity customers. Apps in Power BI will be available in preview to Power BI Pro and Premium Per User customers, as well as Microsoft Fabric capacity customers. Pro and Premium Per User customers will also have access to Fabric Database capabilities, enabling them to build applications that support both analytical and transactional scenarios. This brings AI-assisted app creation to Power BI users through their existing licensing options.

Our community is already bringing some creative ideas to life. Explore some examples from Microsoft and the community in the Fabric apps gallery today.

Figure: Creating an app using natural language in Power BI Desktop.

 

Figure: A community created app by Jon Sandman that shows football statistics and match replays for coaches.

Expanding the semantic layer

The semantic layer is an organization's most strategic asset. More than 22 million Power BI semantic models are in use every day, making Power BI the world’s most widely adopted semantic layer. Increasingly, it also grounds agents, applications, and Microsoft Copilot in that same business meaning.

At FabCon Barcelona, we are sharing an early look at semantic views, allowing users to define governed business metrics and semantics directly where data lives in OneLake and reuse them across and beyond Fabric. Our goal is to bring semantics closer to where the data lives while making it open, reusable, and interoperable.

We are also pleased to affirm our commitment to Apache Ossie (incubating), a community-led effort to establish a vendor-neutral standard for exchanging semantic metadata across analytics, AI, and BI platforms. Working with Snowflake and the broader industry, we’re helping customers define semantic context once and reuse it across ecosystems without duplicating data or business logic. Our collaboration with Snowflake currently focuses on cross-platform semantic-layer conversion. Looking ahead, we’re committed to advancing Apache Ossie through our deep semantic-modeling expertise, establishing DAX as an Ossie-recognized query language and expanding support for ontologies, enabling platform-agnostic operational intelligence.

Figure: Semantic views provide governed business context across analytics, applications, and AI experiences.

Bringing semantic models into M365 Copilot

Fabric IQ in Microsoft Copilot Cowork and Microsoft Copilot Chat are now generally available. Users can ask business questions in Copilot Chat and receive trusted answers grounded in governed Power BI reports and semantic models, with Copilot inferring which report or model is right for the question. In Cowork, Power BI content participates directly in long running and asynchronous tasks.

The same Microsoft Copilot experience is also coming directly to Copilot in Power BI, allowing you to use your M365 data for richer responses. Fabric IQ MCP is entering general availability, so creators can use the same conversational analytics in their own development environments and external MCP clients. You can read more details about this update in our Fabric IQ in Microsoft 365 Copilot Cowork documentation.

Looking ahead

Power BI’s evolution has always been shaped by the community and the millions of creators, analysts, developers, and business users who build with it every day. Your ideas, feedback, and ingenuity have pushed us to make business intelligence more accessible, trusted, and connected to the decisions that matter. Thank you for building this community—and for continuing to challenge us to imagine what comes next.

You can catch all our announcements in detail in the Power BI September 2026 monthly roll-up blog. We invite you to help shape this next chapter—share your feedback with us, shape our roadmap, and meet us in person at Fabric Community Conference and Ignite!

From new Copilot and AI experiences to reporting, modeling, data connectivity, developer enhancements, and mobile updates, we're sharing the latest innovations designed to help you build, analyze, and act on your data more effectively. Whether you're joining us in person or following along from afar, this roundup is your guide to everything new across Power BI this month.

General 

Deprecation of Old File Picker experience in Power BI Desktop

In April we deprecated the old file picker experience in Power BI Desktop. Starting in October, users using versions of Power BI Desktop from March 2026 or earlier will no longer be able to save and share Power BI files to OneDrive and SharePoint. Please ensure you update Power BI Desktop to keep using this functionality.

Copilot and AI 

Power BI Agentic Experiences (Generally Available)

Agentic development in Power BI is real, and it is already delivering value: whether you are starting from scratch with greenfield projects or building upon existing solutions in brownfield scenarios, BI developers can delegate the work to an agent, review the result, and refine it rather than starting from scratch every time.

What makes this work is tools and context. Through Work IQ and Fabric IQ, the agent grounds its work in your business context—your data, your semantics, and the way your organization operates. Through skills—published by Microsoft in skills-for-fabric, shared by the community, or personalized by your own team—it also picks up your development context: the modeling and reporting practices, conventions, and workflows your team expects.

Through tools such as the Power BI Authoring MCP server and the Power BI Desktop Bridge CLI, the agent can act on that context: reading and changing semantic models and reports directly, reloading its edits in Power BI tools, and reviewing its own work. Point an agent at a requirements document or a screenshot of the layout you want, describe what you need, and the agent can help accelerate the initial authoring pass, which you can then review and refine.

Figure: Animated GIF showing the creation of a Power BI report based on a remote semantic model using Modeling MCP, the Modeling skill, and report authoring skills.

What's available today

  • The powerbi-authoring plugin in microsoft/skills-for-fabric bundling the semantic modeling and reporting agent skills and tools. It was recently updated to support report authoring for remote semantic models in Power BI service and an expanded range of supported report visuals, including custom visuals.
  • To learn more, refer to the Power BI skills documentation.
  • The local Power BI Authoring MCP server allows the agent to edit semantic models in Power BI Desktop.
  • To learn more, refer to the Power BI Authoring MCP documentation.
  • Power BI Desktop Bridge lets an agent reload changes in a running instance of Power BI Desktop and capture screenshots to check its own work.
  • To learn more, refer to the Power BI Desktop Bridge documentation.
  • Browser-based validation for remote report editing, so the agent can validate a report using a headless browser (an automated browser that runs without a visible user interface). Removing the local Power BI Desktop dependency allows the full authoring loop to run without Power BI Desktop, extending the agentic experience to Mac users and others who do not rely on a local installation.

To learn more and get started, refer to the Power BI agentic documentation. 

Microsoft 365 Copilot is coming to Power BI (Preview)

Copilot experiences have emerged across the applications people use every day, bringing AI closer to the work happening in each product. But this can also feel fragmented, with different entry points, separate conversations, and uncertainty about which Copilot agent to use.

Our goal is to create a consistent Copilot experience that is available wherever people work. People should not have to leave the application they are using to find it. Microsoft 365 Copilot should be available within their experience, carry relevant context across experiences, and connect to the specialized intelligence of each product.

We’re taking an important step toward that goal with a preview of Microsoft 365 Copilot integrated directly into Power BI and Microsoft Fabric.

This integration gives users a familiar place to bring together business context and trusted data. Shared conversation history lets them continue a discussion as they move between Microsoft 365 Copilot experiences instead of starting over in each application.

Figure:Screenshot of Copilot Chat integrated into the Power BI experience, including integration with Work IQ.

In Power BI, a question no longer has to stop with the numbers in a report. A sales leader could use Fabric IQ to identify which regions are behind plan, then use Work IQ to connect the results with customer emails, meetings, account plans, and documents. They could summarize the complete picture and even kick off actions and tasks in Cowork, all from inside Power BI. This work context and ability to move directly from insight to action were not available in the standalone Power BI Copilot experience.

Figure:Screenshot of the Cowork integration into the Power BI experience, highlighting the full Microsoft 365 experience embedded into Power BI.

A new setting in the Fabric admin portal will determine whether this integration is available by enabling or disabling its entry point in the navigation pane. It will be off by default, giving administrators time to evaluate the experience before introducing it to their organization. Administrators can enable it when they are ready and disable it if they need to pause access.

This setting is independent of the existing setting for standalone Power BI Copilot. If both settings are enabled, users with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license will see entry points for both experiences, and standalone Power BI Copilot will continue to appear on Home. If standalone Power BI Copilot is disabled and Microsoft 365 Copilot is enabled, users will see only the Microsoft 365 Copilot entry point.

During the initial preview, the integrated experience is available only to users with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license. These users receive the full Copilot Chat experience in Power BI and Fabric, bringing together Fabric data through Fabric IQ and relevant Microsoft 365 context through Work IQ. Existing permissions and governance controls continue to determine which content each user can access.

Support for a broader Fabric audience will follow. This expansion will give Fabric users without a Microsoft 365 Copilot license access to an integrated Copilot experience tailored to their available capabilities. The experience may differ from the full licensed offering, but it will extend Fabric IQ and conversational data experiences to more types of Fabric users.

The preview will roll out with the setting turned off by default, with administrators choosing when to enable it for their organization.

This is an important step toward one Copilot that meets people wherever they work, connecting the context surrounding each decision with trusted business data.

To learn more, refer to the Copilot in Power BI documentation.

Power BI data answers in Microsoft Copilot Chat (Generally Available)

Users can find and ask questions about Power BI reports and semantic models directly from Microsoft 365 Copilot. They can search for relevant Power BI content, attach a report or provide a link, and ask questions in natural language.

Figure: Microsoft Copilot Chat featuring a data answer coming from a Power BI report, cited.

Powered by Fabric IQ, the experience uses the data, measures, relationships, and business logic already defined in Power BI to provide grounded answers. Users can also bring Power BI insights into conversations that include their Microsoft 365 work context, such as emails, meetings, and documents.

Microsoft 365 Copilot now supports Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies and information protection controls for this experience. This helps organizations adopt conversational analytics while applying their existing policies for identifying, classifying, and protecting sensitive data. The experience continues to respect existing Power BI permissions and Microsoft 365 governance controls. Users can only access Power BI content they are authorized to view, and administrators retain control over whether Fabric data is available in Microsoft 365 Copilot.

Organizations can use Power BI data answering in Microsoft 365 Copilot with production support and service commitments. This milestone makes it easier for users to bring trusted business data into the flow of work without leaving Microsoft 365 Copilot or creating a separate agent.

To learn more, refer to the Fabric IQ in Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat (Frontier) documentation.

Fabric IQ Plugin in Microsoft 365 Copilot Cowork (Generally Available)

Power BI data is available where multi-step work happens, so a business question, the analysis behind it, and the follow-up it triggers stay in one place.

To ground a task in Power BI, users can search for relevant content, attach a report, or paste a link to a report or semantic model. Questions are answered using the data, measures, relationships, and business logic already defined in the semantic model. Coverage now extends to reports published through organizational apps, with improvements to content discovery, large model handling, schema selection, Verified Answers, and row-level value search.

The plugin also carries forward the governance controls organizations rely on in Power BI:

  • Existing access controls: Power BI permissions and row-level security determine which reports and semantic models each user can reach.
  • Citations and sensitivity labels: Responses cite the Power BI content behind an answer and surface the Microsoft Purview Information Protection label applied to it, so users can see where a number came from and how it is classified.
  • From insight to action: With Fabric IQ, users can analyze Power BI reports using natural language, uncover key findings, and put those findings to work right away in Cowork. Whether they are summarizing business performance, investigating a trend, or answering a data question, Fabric IQ turns trusted organizational data into outcomes.

To learn more about supported scenarios, setup, and current considerations, refer to the Fabric IQ in Microsoft 365 Copilot Cowork documentation.

For licensing and pricing information, refer to Microsoft 365 Copilot plans and pricing.

Build Fabric Apps more easily in GitHub Copilot App (Preview)

Fabric Apps were introduced in June as an AI-first way to build custom web apps with Microsoft Fabric as the backend. This month we’re excited to share that building these Fabric Apps on your governed data has become even easier with the GitHub Copilot App, which gives you a natural language chat interface instead of a command-line interface.

Figure: GitHub Copilot App chat interface.

To try it out, start by downloading the GitHub Copilot App. Then navigate to Customize > Plugins > Rayfin, and select Install to enable our dedicated plugin:

Figure: Installing Rayfin plugin in GitHub Copilot App.

Once the plugin is enabled, simply start a new chat and work with Copilot to help plan your Fabric data app. After you review and approve the plan, ask the agent to execute it and specify the workspace where you want to deploy the app.

Figure: Example New York Taxi app.

We look forward to seeing the amazing apps you build! Check out our community gallery for inspiration.

Enhanced Report Consumption Copilot with Fabric IQ

When viewing a Power BI report, you can enable Fabric IQ from the Copilot pane to better answer complex questions about your data. This enhancement merges existing Fabric IQ capabilities into Power BI Copilot report viewing mode, allowing Copilot to use a multi-step approach to evaluate data in the semantic model and refine its approach when generating a response.

Figure: Fabric IQ enabled in Power BI Copilot report pane (viewing mode) to answer a data question with a supporting textual answer and visualization.

With Fabric IQ enabled, Copilot can:

  • Provide better answers to questions about your data based on detailed reasoning capabilities directly into the report viewing experience.
  • Show reasoning steps to help you understand how Copilot provided an answer.
  • Generate Fabric visuals to help you further analyze your data. Answers can include column, bar, stacked, line, area, pie, donut, scatter visuals.
  • Provide the underlying DAX query and data table used to generate a response.
Figure: GIF illustrating how to enable Fabric IQ in Power BI Copilot report pane (viewing mode) to answer data questions.

To learn more, refer to the Ask Copilot questions about your data documentation.

New control for Copilot access to semantic models

Power BI now provides semantic model editors with greater control over how Copilot can be used with their data. Users with write permissions can block read-only users from accessing a semantic model through Copilot and Microsoft’s remote MCP tools, supporting governance, compliance, and access-control requirements.

The setting applies across Copilot experiences that query the semantic model, including Power BI Copilot experiences; Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat and Cowork; and data agents, remote Fabric MCP servers, and Power BI MCP servers. When disabled, users with read-only access won't be able to access that semantic model through these experiences. By default, the setting remains enabled to preserve the current behavior.

This setting appears in the Copilot section with the following description: “Allow any person with read-only access to use AI (i.e. Copilot, Microsoft’s MCP tools) on the model and its related reports.”

Figure: Setting that allows people with read-only permission to use AI experiences with the semantic model and its related reports.

This update gives organizations a clear and enforceable way to control AI access to semantic model data while maintaining flexibility for semantic model editors.

To learn more, refer to the Use Copilot with Semantic Models in Power BI documentation.

Remote Power BI Authoring MCP Server (Preview)

The Power BI Authoring MCP enables AI applications to create and modify semantic models in Fabric workspaces, without installing or maintaining anything local. This release also unblocks Mac users that want to use the Power BI Authoring MCP, because the server runs remotely and does not require local binaries.

Use the following endpoint in AI applications such as GitHub Copilot App:

https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/mcp/powerbi/authoring

Figure: Power BI Remote MCP Server configuration in GitHub Copilot App.

The local Power BI Authoring MCP server, released in November 2025, remains generally available. It remains an option when an agent needs to work with Power BI Desktop, Power BI Project (PBIP) or TMDL files on disk. The local and remote servers support the same authoring capabilities.

We recommend using the remote server when local development is not required, such as when creating a Direct Lake semantic model in a Fabric workspace.

In the following example, the AI agent uses one tool call to create a Direct Lake semantic model connected to a Fabric Lakehouse:

Figure: Using Power BI Remote MCP to create a Direct Lake semantic model.

To learn more, refer to the Power BI Authoring MCP server documentation.

Reporting 

New Report Ribbon on the web (Preview)

The Report ribbon is now available on the web, providing a consistent experience for report consumption and authoring that more closely matches Power BI Desktop. The ribbon organizes commands into clear, easy-to-navigate tabs, making it easier for users to discover features, interact with reports, and complete editing and authoring tasks directly in the browser. It also introduces the new Design ribbon and additional capabilities that were previously unavailable on the web, such as Format Painter.

This milestone brings greater consistency to Power BI report-authoring experiences and marks an important step toward a seamless, end-to-end reporting workflow on the web. As web authoring capabilities continue to expand, users will be able to accomplish more of their reporting tasks directly in the browser, enabling a more streamlined, productive workflow.

Figure: New report ribbon on the web.

Enable the Try the new ribbon (preview) at the top of the page to explore the new experience. You can disable the setting to return to the previous ribbon.

To learn more, refer to the Report Ribbon on the web documentation.

Live Visual Sharing in Outlook on the web (Preview)

For years, sharing data through email has been stagnant. You could send a screenshot, but it immediately became stale. You could attach a report link, but recipients had to leave their workflow to find the context they needed. And every follow-up question often meant another screenshot, another export, or another email thread.

Now, we're bringing a new way to share Power BI insights directly in the flow of work with Live Visual Sharing in Outlook. With Live Visual Sharing, you can insert a Power BI visual into Outlook on the web and share it as a live, interactive experience. Recipients can view and interact with the visual directly in Outlook while staying connected to the latest underlying data.

Figure: A live Power BI visual in Outlook on the web.

When a live visual is shared, Outlook renders an interactive version of the Power BI visual. Rather than embedding a static image, the experience remains connected to the source report and retrieves current data when viewed.

Recipients can:

  • Interact with the visual directly in Outlook on the web.
  • Access tooltips and explore data points.
  • See filters and slicers applied at the time of sharing.
  • View refresh information and data context.
  • Navigate back to the source report when deeper analysis is needed.

The result is a richer conversation around data, directly within Outlook.

Sharing a live visual is simple:

  1. Open a Power BI report in the service.
  2. Select a visual to share, then select More options in the upper-right corner.
  3. Select Share.
Figure: Share option in Power BI.
  1. Select Link to this visual.
Figure: Link to this visual as part of the share dialog.
  1. A pop-up will appear asking if you want to use the current view (apply existing filters and slicers) or not.
  2. After selecting Create Link, the link is copied to your clipboard.
Figure: Before copying the link, you can configure the view in this dialog.
  1. Open Outlook on the web. This experience is not available in the Outlook desktop app. Create a new email.
  2. Paste the link in the email. The visual renders in loop after a few seconds! You can also share the same link in a Loop page, and the visual will also be rendered.
Figure: An unfurled Power BI visual in Outlook on the web.

By combining Power BI, Outlook, and Loop-powered experiences, we're bringing data closer to where collaboration happens. Live Visual Sharing can support more informed, data-driven conversations in Outlook.

To learn more about Live Visual Sharing in Outlook, refer to the Share live Power BI visuals documentation.

More control and context in Power BI Home (Generally Available)

Power BI Home now provides additional context and personalization options to help users discover the right content more efficiently. With new freshness indicators and customizable list views, you can quickly identify the most relevant reports and semantic models, prioritize the metadata that matters most, and tailor the experience to fit your workflow.

Find the right content more easily

Discover the right content more easily with new Data Refreshed and Modified Date columns in Power BI Home. By bringing the freshness signals already familiar from workspace list views into Home, users can more easily spot recently updated reports and semantic models, distinguish between similar items, and quickly find the content that matters most. Whether you're checking for the latest business updates or deciding which refreshed report to open, you can navigate with greater confidence and less guesswork.

Figure: Power BI Home showing two new columns for Data refreshed and Modified date.

Customize your Home list view

Not every user, team, or organization relies on the same signals to discover content. With Column Options, you can show or hide metadata, drag and reorder columns to prioritize the information you use most, and reset to the default view at any time. Whether you rely on freshness signals, endorsements, sensitivity labels, or location information, you can tailor Home to match your workflow.

Figure: Power BI Home showing new column options dropdown.

To learn more, refer to the Power BI Home documentation.

Set and reset column widths in table and matrix (Generally Available)

You can now right-click a column header in a table or matrix and select Set column width to specify its width in pixels. This option helps report viewers improve readability and fit the information they need within the available space, without changing the report author’s design or affecting other viewers. Changes made by viewers last only for the current viewing session. To restore the width defined by the report author, right-click the column header and select Reset column width.

Figure: Set or reset the width of an individual table or matrix column from its context menu.

To learn more, refer to the Adjust column width in Power BI tables documentation.

Visual calculations for small multiples (Generally Available)

You can now use visual calculations in visuals with small multiples. Approximate Distinct Count comes to Import and Direct Lake (Preview)

Distinct count is one of the most resource-intensive operations in any analytical engine. As data cardinality grows, so do CPU and memory usage, often slowing down your interactive reports.

APPROXIMATEDISTINCTCOUNT already offered a faster alternative for DirectQuery sources such as Azure SQL, Synapse, BigQuery, Databricks, and Snowflake. This month we're extending support to Import, Direct Lake on OneLake, and Direct Lake on SQL semantic models.

DAX = APPROXIMATEDISTINCTCOUNT(<columnName>)

Figure: Model View in Power BI Service showing tables, relationships, and the properties panel for editing a DirectQuery semantic model.

How it works and when to use it

Instead of scanning every single unique value, APPROXIMATEDISTINCTCOUNT calculates a highly accurate estimate of unique values with a standard error rate of ~1.6%. In return, you get faster query execution times.

  • Best for high-cardinality columns: Use it on columns with millions of unique values (such as transaction IDs, user IDs, or timestamps) where an approximate result can reduce the resources required to calculate distinct values.
  • Keep standard DISTINCTCOUNT for low-cardinality data: Stick to exact counts for smaller attributes like Country, Category, or Status, where standard calculation is already fast, or for financial metrics where absolute precision is required.

Swap APPROXIMATEDISTINCTCOUNT into your heaviest measures today and let us know how much speed you gain on your models!

Accelerate text searches in your semantic models with String Indexing (Preview)

String Indexing for Power BI semantic models is coming soon! If your reports rely heavily on text fields, such as product names, customer comments, or long descriptions, you’ve likely faced slow performance when users search or filter on large semantic models. String Indexing is designed to improve text-search performance in supported semantic models.

Why String Indexing?

Common text operations like DAX functions (SEARCH(), CONTAINSSTRING()) and advanced text slicers in reports traditionally scan data row-by-row. As datasets grow, these scans slow down query times.

String Indexing builds specialized indexes so the engine can locate matching text more efficiently, which can improve report responsiveness for both Import and Direct Lake semantic models.

Indexing modes

You can configure String Indexing via model metadata to fit your workload needs:

  • Auto Mode: Automatically builds the index on the first query execution for a qualifying column. The index does not persist in storage; it remains in memory only while the column is loaded and will be rebuilt on subsequent queries if evicted. Ideal for smaller models.
  • Full Mode: Builds and persists the index during scheduled data refreshes. While refresh times and model size may slightly increase, users enjoy consistently fast query performance right out of the box.

Get started

String Indexing requires a semantic model running at 1707 compatibility level. During this initial preview phase, indexing can be configured through TMDL on the web or XMLA metadata. Desktop support and a dedicated UI experience within Power BI are planned for a future release to simplify setup.

Introducing Full-Text Search in Power BI Semantic Models (Preview)

Full-Text Indexing for Power BI semantic models is coming soon! While traditional string searches look for exact character matches, Full-Text Indexing enables a more intelligent search experience based on the meaning of words and natural language concepts. This capability powers two new DAX functions, TEXTCONTAINS() and TEXTSIMILARITY(), making it easier than ever to analyze large volumes of textual data directly in your semantic models.

Why Full-Text Indexing?

Business data increasingly contains rich text content such as customer feedback, support tickets, product descriptions, incident summaries, and knowledge articles. Searching this data using traditional string matching often requires exact matches and can miss relevant results due to differences in spelling, word forms, or phrasing.

Full-Text Indexing builds a specialized search index at the column level, allowing semantic models to understand words rather than just character sequences. This enables advanced search experiences such as:

  • Finding related words through linguistic analysis (for example, run, running, and runs)
  • Matching singular and plural variations automatically
  • Ignoring common stop words such as "the" or "and"
  • Supporting phrase-based searches
  • Tolerating minor spelling mistakes through fuzzy matching
  • Enabling semantic similarity search scenarios

Getting Started

FTS Indexing requires a semantic model running at 1708 compatibility level. During this initial preview phase, indexing can be configured through TMDL on the web or XMLA metadata. Desktop support and a dedicated UI experience within Power BI are planned for a future release to simplify setup.

Figure: Setting up the “fullTextIndexingbehavior” property to full in TMDL view in the web.

New DAX functions

Full-Text Indexing is required for two new DAX functions:

  • TEXTCONTAINS()
    • Returns TRUE when a text value matches a search expression using full-text search semantics rather than simple substring matching. It supports multiple search modes, including keyword matching, phrase matching, and fuzzy matching for typo tolerance
    • TextContains(<WithinTextColumn>, <SearchText>, [MatchMode])
  • Example: "Show me all reviews that mention spa." The review either matches or it doesn't.Figure: Example of the new TEXTCONTAINS() DAX function in DAX query view.
  • TEXTSIMILARITY()
    • Returns a relevance score indicating how well the text in <WithinTextColumn> matches <SearchText>. It enables similarity-based text comparisons, helping identify records that are semantically related even when they do not contain the exact same words.
    • TextSimilarity(<WithinTextColumn>, <SearchText> [, <MatchMode>])
  • Example: "Show me the 10 reviews most relevant to 'good breakfast'." Reviews mentioning both terms prominently rank higher than reviews that only partially match.
Figure: Example of the new TEXTSIMILARITY() DAX function in DAX query view.

Learn more about these two new DAX functions (TEXTCONTAINS, TEXTSIMILARITY) in our documentation.

Full-Text Indexing is supported for both Import and Direct Lake models, with Full mode recommended (during Preview) for the best out-of-the-box performance and user experience.

powerbi_blog:3e1818ad92ea.title: Modern Power BI architecture choices for reporting on Azure Databricks: A performance benchmark for Power BI storage modes
powerbi_blog:3e1818ad92ea.excerpt:
Many enterprise Power BI semantic models use Azure Databricks as a data source. When building these models, developers and architects face an early and consequential decision: which storage mode to use. Cost, security, and ease of development and tuning all factor in — but report performance is probably the most important of them, because reports that are slow to load are one of the most common causes of end-user dissatisfaction.

In practice, that decision is often made on intuition rather than evidence. To help change that, we've published a new white paper, Modern Power BI Architecture Choices for Reporting on Azure Databricks, benchmarking four ways of serving the same Delta tables to a Power BI report:

  • Direct Lake on OneLake — over Delta tables in a Fabric lakehouse or warehouse

  • Direct Lake on mirrored Unity Catalog tables — shortcuts, no copy

  • DirectQuery — on a Databricks SQL warehouse

  • Composite Model on Databricks — DirectQuery combined with Import-mode aggregations

Figure: The four Power BI storage modes benchmarked to evaluate their impact on report performance and scalability.

What the results suggest: there's no universal winner — but there are clear patterns.

Direct Lake on OneLake performed well across the widest range of situations in this benchmark. It's highly competitive at smaller and mid-size volumes, and for the typical Power BI workload — where reports are used repeatedly throughout the day — it delivers interactive performance without extra modeling effort.

At the top end of the volume curve, the picture shifts. With billions of rows, a Composite Model with aggregations was the fastest and most consistent pattern, staying sub-100ms on queries the aggregation tables can resolve. The caveat is equally clear: that advantage doesn't extend to queries that fall through to the underlying DirectQuery source, so the payoff depends on how well your aggregations match real user behavior.

These are just the headline findings — the detailed results vary considerably by data volume, cache state, filter scenario, and query type. We'd encourage you to read the white paper for the full picture before deciding on a pattern.

One thing worth noting up front: this is a point-in-time comparison as of June/July 2026, and both platforms are moving quickly. It also measures the end-user query experience within Power BI, rather than raw database execution speed. Treat it as a guide for running your own testing, on your own data.

Explore the white paper for a full walkthrough of through each pattern in detail — the test setup, what was measured, and how results break down by data volume, cache state, and query type.

Visit the Power BI download center to access the paper and other related resources.

simon_whiteley:a78109a5a174.title: Push or Pull? What Bad Design Reveals About Our Data Platforms
simon_whiteley:a78109a5a174.excerpt:
I hate Norman doors. And I hate the people who design them.

What is a Norman door? It's pure evil is what it is. Look at this picture and answer me this — should you push, or should you pull this door?

Handles... pull surely? But there's also handles on the other side? Hmm....

I've been watching a lot of Subway Takes, and thinking about what I'd say to Kareem if he ever took a break from interviewing the Jennifer Lopezes and Rizzlers of the world. It's the above. It's clearly pull! This big old handle is sending the word PULL to my brain, in block capitals, unambiguously. And so you go to pull it and — they lied to me, betrayed me, it's a push?? And they've put handles on both sides?? Now I'm left standing there like some sort of moron. Look at this shmuck, he doesn't even know how to open a door!

And that — that little flush of heat up the back of my neck — is the actual crime. Not that the door didn't open. That it made me the idiot for a mistake that was engineered, by a professional, on purpose. It is one of the highest forms of everyday humiliation that someone got paid to insert into my life. The door failed, and somehow I'm the one standing there embarrassed.

And there are literally only two options! A door has a vocabulary of exactly two words — push, pull (sliding doors, the heretic's choice, not permitting) — and whoever installed it took one look and thought "sure, why not, this makes complete sense" and they just... installed it like that, completely wrong, and went home. All I know is that in my hand is not a door handle, it is failure.

This is not a hypothetical, these doors are out to get me. Pulling on one this weekend was the final straw — and so, saddled with this burden, the shame still fresh, I find myself in front of my computer ready for the first in a short run of posts on how we build platforms people can actually use... inspired, of all things, by a door. I didn't actually know the thing had a name for the longest time (shoutout to 99% Invisible for bringing this to my attention) — but the fact it comes from a 1988 book, Don Norman's The Design of Everyday Things, tells us that in forty years we still haven't cracked the human-centric design challenge that is opening doors.

A "coffeepot for masochists", the cover image of The Design of Everyday Things.

Now, here's where I have to be honest about how this post got away from me. I went to dig out that book to check my details, and got ambushed by the cover: a bright red coffeepot with the handle and the spout on the same side — a thing that can't pour, can't be held, can't do the one job a coffeepot has. Norman didn't draw it. A French artist named Jacques Carelman did, for a 1969 book of his own — Catalogue d'objets introuvables, "a catalogue of unfindable objects." It's a mock mail-order catalogue of things that look on face value completely usable and yet are completely absurd. Taps plumbed in a row into one pipe. Two bicycles with their front wheels welded shut. Each one lovingly drawn, described, numbered — and not one of them works.

And that's the moment this post got bigger than doors. I set out to write about one misleading door, and the book about the door handed me a whole catalogue of things that don't work — the door's just the first plate in it. I've read a lot of definitions of a data platform. This is the best one, and it's French, and it's from 1969. So, allez.

The Confession Taped to the Door

Think about what people do to a Norman door once they've given up fixing it: they tape a paper sign above the handle that says PUSH. That sign is a confession — it exists only because the door is not door-ing — and it doesn't even work, because your hand is on the handle before your eyes reach the word. You yank it and bathe in the shame either way.

Even worse, a permanent testament to its wrongness.

Now look at any data platform. READMEs, wikis, architecture diagrams — and if I squint into the background of someone's camera on Teams, I'm fairly sure they've etched the release process into their wall. Every one of them is a paper PUSH sign taped over a handle that lies. We call it documentation. It's a monument to bad design. Allow me to add it to the catalogue.

Pl. 12 Catalogue d'objets introuvables
README.md data-platform-core · updated 8 months ago

data-platform-core

The platform. Please read this entire file before touching anything. (You won't.)

Getting started

1. Clone the repo.

2. Do not commit without --no-verify. The unit tests are blocking us and we don't know why.

3. Ask Dave.

Pipelines

Orchestration_Master — does nothing. Do NOT delete it. Things break and no one knows why.

test_pipeline_v2 — this is the real one. Yes, it runs in prod. Yes, "test". Don't ask.

Known issues

• If the build fails, re-run it. If it fails again, re-run it. The third run usually works.

• sp-dev-readonly has read-write in prod. This is load-bearing. Do not "fix" it.

• The Confluence page contradicts this README. This README is also wrong. Trust neither.

Onboarding

Good luck. Post in #platform-help (avg. response time: 3 business days) and someone will tell you to ask Dave.

Manual for a machine that cannot be operated. — Complete, current, and of no use to anyone.

A push/pull door gives you two ways to be wrong. A platform gives you a thousand — which doesn't make it better designed, only better at hiding. Because a platform isn't one Norman door. It's the whole catalogue: the README that documents a thing you still can't use, the pipeline named for a job it doesn't do, the access request you can raise and never get granted — every one an objet introuvable, photographed to look usable, lovingly maintained, quietly impossible. And whether it was one architect, a committee, or a snowball of small sensible decisions no one can account for now, the rule's the same: when the lived reality of a thing doesn't match what its design says, something has gone awry, and there is usually a someone or someones sat behind that.

If we can't get it right for a door — two options, forty years of warning — what hope does anyone have walking into a platform, whether they're an architect, an engineer, or the poor soul who just wants to run one query, of not coming away wondering if they're the moron?

A Good Door Disappears

We already know what a good door looks like, and it isn't a door with better instructions. A door that works needs no sign; its shape tells you what to do. A flat plate gives your hand nothing to grab, so you push. A bar you can wrap a hand around asks to be pulled. Norman calls that honesty an affordance — the shape telling the truth about the job. You don't remember the last good door you walked through, because a good door disappears. We only notice design when it betrays us.

A Norman door is the shape lying. The handle says pull, the mechanism says push, and you're the one who ends up looking stupid for it.

A platform has a shape too, long before anyone opens the docs: its structure, its names, what it puts in reach and what it buries. A Norman platform is one where that shape lies — the CI ticks green but silently fails; the pipeline called Orchestration_Master does nothing except call test_pipeline_v2, which does everything; the read-only Dev service principal that, surprise, has read-write in Prod. Each is a handle on a push door. Each is another plate in the catalogue.
